extracted.intended_audience: media scholars, journalism students, and news editors
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and descriptive dimensions that determine newsworthiness and how events/actors are selected and framed in national television and newsmagazine coverage. Covers activity-types, symbolic frames (nation/society), and demographic/ideological selection biases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Government conflicts and disagreements
rubrics_metrics.description: About 15 percent of domestic news is given over to disagreements and conflicts within and between parts of government and the public officials who personify them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Often focuses on the president and conflicts with Congress; specific topics vary over time (since the 1970s primarily economic policy). This category is numerically stable year-to-year and is central because the news emphasizes conflict.

rubrics_metrics.name: Government decisions, proposals, and ceremonies
rubrics_metrics.description: A somewhat smaller proportion of stories deals with less conflict-laden government activities, reporting government decisions, proposals, and ceremonies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mostly announcements by the president or executive-branch officials of new policies; includes Congressional approval of legislation and Supreme Court decisions. Journalists sometimes call these 'input' stories (announcements) as compared to rarer 'output' stories (implementation). Some of these later become conflict news.

rubrics_metrics.name: Government personnel changes (including campaigning)
rubrics_metrics.description: News about appointments, resignations, dismissals of high public officials and campaign activities of presidential hopefuls.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In newsmagazines this is often the most numerically frequent government story; includes cabinet secretaries, federal agency heads, and occasionally state/local officials. Campaign activity coverage varies by medium and election cycle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protests, violent and nonviolent
rubrics_metrics.description: Demonstrations and disturbances—around 10 percent of domestic activities in some samples—most often related to racial issues (excluding some tallies of anti-war protest).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If protest is defined as citizen-government conflict and combined with intragovernment conflict, political conflict becomes the single most frequent activity. Including anti-war protest would raise proportions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Crimes, scandals, and investigations
rubrics_metrics.description: Almost a fifth of domestic activities are about crimes, scandals, and their investigations; in some years (e.g., 1975) this can be the most newsworthy category due to extraordinary events.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Typical stories often concerned financial misbehavior of government officials and related investigations, trials, and exposés (e.g., Watergate/CIA). Scandals can temporarily dominate coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disasters, actual and averted
rubrics_metrics.description: Television and magazines give attention to small and large disasters and human efforts to avert, control, and explain them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Long-lasting natural catastrophes or disasters with heavy death tolls get magazine coverage; small disasters are covered on TV unless victims are 'Unknowns' (i.e., anonymous/low-profile). Human-interest and heroism in averting disasters are emphasized.

rubrics_metrics.name: Innovation and tradition ('first and last' news)
rubrics_metrics.description: News about social, cultural, or technological innovations and the decline/disappearance of traditional practices—often 'firsts' or 'lasts'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: first woman in an occupation, debut of a new device. Related category: record-setting activities (new highs/lows in statistics) which receive special prominence. Coverage also attends to disappearance of traditions (final trips, abolished uniforms).

rubrics_metrics.name: National ceremonies
rubrics_metrics.description: Events construed as national ceremonies—presidential elections, moon landing, Bicentennial, official visits—are especially newsworthy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ceremonies represent the nation or national identity; media frequently break routine formats to cover them at greater length (TV 'specials', magazine special sections). Tragic events (assassinations) are often treated as national ceremonies and indicators of national cohesion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nation and society as recurring subjects
rubrics_metrics.description: The news is principally about the nation (operationally defined as the federal government) and, to a lesser degree, society (soft news/features).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stories often treat the nation as a unit and judge events by their consequences for the country as a whole; the presidency frequently symbolizes the nation. Coverage privileges nationwide institutions that are 'nationalized' by the media.

rubrics_metrics.name: Symbolic complexes as framing devices
rubrics_metrics.description: News is organized around symbolic complexes (Government, Law, Religion, Science, Medicine, Business and Labor, Education, the Arts, etc.) which become section topics and interpretive frames.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: New complexes are added as actors/activities emerge (e.g., Races, Sexes, Cities, Youth, Economy, Family, Environment). Cover stories and documentaries commonly use these complexes to link actors/activities/statistics to broader social conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Threats to symbolic complexes signal newsworthiness
rubrics_metrics.description: Threats to the symbolic complexes that comprise the nation (e.g., Presidency, Economy, Family) are made newsworthy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stories commonly frame events as testing the nation's character or cohesion (nation-as-individual rhetoric). Foreign policy stories may present the nation as a unit vis-à-vis other nations; domestic events are often judged by national consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conflict as the dominant narrative frame
rubrics_metrics.description: Because much news is about disagreements and disputes, conflict frames dominate and produce an overall picture of a conflicted nation/society.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combining protests, intragovernment conflict, and other disputes often makes political conflict the most frequent activity in news. This preference for conflict shapes selection and prominence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Events judged against traditional ideals and practices
rubrics_metrics.description: News stories frequently assess contemporary events in relation to traditional ideals or historical practices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include judging resignations or elections as evidence of constitutional effectiveness, or Bicentennial coverage comparing contemporary America to Founding ideals. This tendency can obscure innovations or new solutions by privileging continuity with tradition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Actor selection bias: public officials and upper-middle-class 'Knowns'
rubrics_metrics.description: Main actors in national news are public officials and middle-/upper-middle-class individuals who have positions in national institutions; 'Unknowns' and the poor are less frequently reported.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because news focuses on public roles, actors are often in the top income brackets by role (not by explicit mention of income). Less affluent people appear mainly as protesters, criminals, or victims; coverage privileges people who have entered national institutions or who personify policy issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Race as a principal axis of news division
rubrics_metrics.description: Race (notably black-white relations) became a primary societal division in the news in the late 1960s, driven by ghetto disturbances and integration issues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coverage often centered on integration (schools) and legal/political difficulties of notable black figures. National news tended to feature middle-/upper-middle-class blacks who overcame obstacles; less affluent blacks were more often portrayed as protesters, criminals, or victims. By mid-1970s, racial news shifted toward crime-focused coverage for blacks in some outlets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Class is underreported and culturally reframed
rubrics_metrics.description: Income/class differences are infrequently addressed directly; when they appear, they are often reframed as cultural/lifestyle differences rather than structural class conflict.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journalists avoid terms like 'working class' (Marxist connotations), preferring constructs such as 'Middle American'. News recognizes rough strata (poor/underclass, lower middle, middle, rich) but often universalizes upper-middle-class practices; coverage privileges affluent/professional classes and largely omits sustained attention to poverty or structural class interests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sex (gender) as an emergent principal division
rubrics_metrics.description: In the 1970s, sex/gender became an important division in the news, with coverage of women's liberation and entry of women into formerly male roles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: News emphasizes organized movement activities and the successes of professional women, treating women as a newsworthy minority. Coverage tends to privilege leaders and professionals over working-class feminist concerns; depiction of sex-industry topics (pinups, prostitution) changed less.

rubrics_metrics.name: Age and generational framing
rubrics_metrics.description: Age groups are noted mainly when relevant to politics or protest; generations are treated as symbolic complexes typifying historical periods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Most news concerns middle-aged/older public officials and younger protesters or crime-involved youth. Television runs more features about older people; magazines write more about college-aged youth. Generations are framed by reactions to major historical events (e.g., WWII, 1960s unrest).

rubrics_metrics.name: Ideology spectrum and its media application
rubrics_metrics.description: The news applies an ideological spectrum (from radicals on the Far Left to right-wing extremists on the Far Right) but treats most American political actors as non-ideological shades (liberal, moderate, conservative).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The media favors the moderate core (liberals, moderates, conservatives) and treats extremes less favorably. Ideology is often applied only to clearly ideological actors (e.g., Communists, radicals) and more readily to foreign contexts than to domestic American politics; labeling can be imprecise (e.g., 'liberal' spanning a wide range).
